lessons.title: Ideal Temperature for Fresh Meat Storage
lessons.body:
For fresh meat from cattle, goats, or sheep, the ideal storage temperature is between -1Â°C and 2Â°C. This range keeps meat safe and fresh. At these temperatures, harmful bacteria grow very slowly. If the temperature goes above 4Â°C, bacteria multiply quickly and meat can spoil within hours. If it drops below -2Â°C, the meat may start to freeze, which changes texture and taste. So aim for 0Â°C to 2Â°C for short-term storage (up to 5 days). For longer storage (1-3 weeks), keep it at -1Â°C to 0Â°C. 

In Africa, many cold rooms are cooled by a refrigeration unit. The air temperature inside the room should be checked with a reliable thermometer. Do not rely on the unit's dial alone. Place the thermometer near the meat, not near the door or fan. The temperature can vary by 2-3Â°C from one corner to another. So, use at least two thermometers: one near the door and one at the back. 

Meat from a freshly slaughtered beast is warm (around 37Â°C). Before storing, it must be cooled quickly to below 4Â°C within 24 hours. This is called rapid chilling. If you put warm meat into the cold room, it will raise the room temperature and risk spoiling all the meat. So, always pre-cool meat in a separate chiller or hang it in a cool, ventilated place before moving it into the cold room. 

Humidity also matters. Keep relative humidity between 85% and 90% to prevent the meat from drying out. Too dry, and you lose weight and quality. Too wet, and mould grows. A simple hygrometer can measure humidity. If humidity is low, place shallow pans of clean water on the floor. If too high, improve ventilation. 

Remember, these temperatures are for fresh meat, not frozen. For frozen storage, you need -18Â°C or lower. But this module focuses on fresh meat for 4-10 beasts, which is typical for small butcheries or restaurants. Always keep the cold room door closed. Every time you open it, cold air escapes and warm air enters. Train everyone to be quick. 

Check the temperature at least twice a day, morning and evening. Write it down. If you see the temperature rising above 3Â°C, act immediately. Use the steps in Lesson 4. Your goal is to keep meat safe for your customers and avoid losses. With careful monitoring, your cold room will serve you well.

lessons.title: Using a Thermometer and Data Logger
lessons.body:
A thermometer is your most important tool in the cold room. You need at least two types: a dial thermometer or digital probe thermometer for spot checks, and a data logger for continuous recording. A simple digital probe thermometer costs about 10-20 USD and can be bought from agricultural supply shops or online. A data logger costs 30-100 USD and records temperature every few minutes. 

To use a probe thermometer: first, clean the probe with alcohol or warm soapy water. Insert the probe into the thickest part of a piece of meat, not just the air. Wait 30 seconds for the reading to stabilise. For air temperature, hold the probe in the air away from your body and wait 2 minutes. Record the reading. Do this for at least three different spots: near the door, in the centre, and at the back. 

A data logger is a small device that you place inside the cold room. It has a sensor and memory. Set it to record every 5 or 10 minutes. Some models have a USB port so you can download the data to a computer or phone. Others send alerts by SMS if the temperature goes out of range. This is very useful in Africa where power can be unreliable. If you cannot afford a data logger, use a min-max thermometer. It shows the highest and lowest temperatures since last reset. Reset it every morning. 

Calibrate your thermometers regularly. Once a month, make an ice bath: fill a glass with crushed ice and water, stir, and insert the probe. It should read 0Â°C. If not, adjust or replace. Also check in boiling water (100Â°C at sea level). For every 300 metres above sea level, boiling point drops by 1Â°C. So in Nairobi (1,795m), boiling water is about 94Â°C. 

Keep thermometers clean. Meat juices can carry bacteria. Wipe the probe with a disinfectant wipe after each use. Store thermometers in a clean, dry place. Never leave a thermometer inside the meat for long periods unless it is a permanent probe. 

If you have a data logger, download the data weekly and look for patterns. Maybe the temperature rises every afternoon when the door is opened often. Or at night when the compressor rests. This helps you fix problems before they cause spoilage. Share the data with your workers so they understand the importance of keeping the door closed. 

Finally, always have a backup thermometer. If one breaks, you can still monitor. In remote areas, order spare batteries and probes in advance. A well-monitored cold room saves money and keeps customers happy.

lessons.title: Checking Temperature Twice Daily
lessons.body:
Checking the temperature twice a day is the minimum for safe meat storage. Do it at the same times every day: early morning (before opening the cold room for business) and late afternoon (before closing). This gives you a clear picture of how the cold room performs over 24 hours. If you only check once, you might miss a problem that happens at night. 

Morning check: As soon as you arrive, before opening the door, read the thermometer or data logger. If you have a min-max thermometer, note the lowest temperature from the night. Then open the door and quickly check the meat temperature with a probe. Write down both air and meat temperatures. Also check that the cooling unit is running and there is no ice build-up. 

Afternoon check: About 30 minutes before closing, repeat the process. Compare with the morning reading. A difference of more than 2Â°C means something is wrong. For example, if morning was 1Â°C and afternoon is 4Â°C, the cold room is struggling. Maybe the door was left open, or the condenser is dirty, or there is a power issue. 

Use a log book (see Lesson 6) to record: date, time, air temperature, meat temperature, and your initials. Also note any unusual events: power cut, door left open, defrost cycle, or delivery of warm meat. This record helps you spot trends and prove to customers that you maintain proper conditions. 

If you cannot be there twice a day, train a trusted worker to do it. Give them a simple checklist. For example: 1) Read thermometer, 2) Write number, 3) Check meat, 4) Look at unit, 5) Sign. Make it part of their daily routine. Pay them a small bonus for accuracy. 

In hot African climates, the cold room works harder. During the hottest part of the day (2-4 pm), the temperature may rise slightly. That is normal if it stays below 4Â°C. But if it goes above 5Â°C, take action. You can adjust the thermostat slightly lower, but do not set it below -2Â°C or meat will freeze. 

Remember, twice daily checks are not just a chore. They are your early warning system. A small rise caught early can be fixed with a simple adjustment. A rise caught late can mean thousands of shillings in lost meat. So be consistent. Set an alarm on your phone. Write it on the wall. Make it a habit. 

If you have a data logger, you can check it less often, but still do a physical check twice a day to ensure the logger is working and the door seals are good. Technology can fail, but your eyes and hands are reliable.

lessons.title: What to Do When Temperature Rises
lessons.body:
If you check the temperature and it is above 4Â°C, act immediately. Do not wait. Every hour above 4Â°C allows bacteria to multiply. The first step is to stay calm and find the cause. Common causes: power cut, door left open, dirty condenser coils, faulty thermostat, refrigerant leak, or too much warm meat placed inside. 

Step 1: Check the door. Is it closed properly? Are the seals dirty or torn? If open, close it and wait 30 minutes. Recheck. If the temperature drops back to normal, the problem was the door. Remind everyone to keep it closed. 

Step 2: Check the power. Is the compressor running? Listen for the hum. If no power, check the main switch, fuse box, or generator. If you have a backup generator, start it. If not, you have a few hours before meat spoils. You can use ice blocks or dry ice to keep the cold room cool. For a small cold room (4-10 beasts), you need about 20-30 kg of ice per day. Place ice in trays on the top shelves. 

Step 3: Check the cooling unit. Are the condenser coils dirty? Dust and cobwebs are common in Africa. Clean them with a soft brush and vacuum. Is the evaporator fan running? If not, call a technician. Do not try to repair refrigerant lines yourself. 

Step 4: Check the thermostat setting. Maybe it was accidentally turned up. Set it back to 0Â°C to 2Â°C. Wait 1 hour and recheck. 

Step 5: If the temperature is above 7Â°C for more than 2 hours, the meat may be unsafe. Do not sell it. Cook it immediately and sell as cooked meat, or discard. Never refreeze meat that has been above 7Â°C for more than 2 hours. 

Step 6: If the temperature is between 4Â°C and 7Â°C for less than 2 hours, you can quickly cool it back down. Move meat to a backup chiller if available. Otherwise, keep the door closed and monitor every 30 minutes. 

Step 7: After the crisis, find the root cause. If it was a power cut, consider buying a generator or solar backup. If it was a dirty condenser, set a monthly cleaning schedule. If it was a faulty thermostat, replace it. 

Always have a plan. Write an emergency contact list: electrician, refrigeration technician, ice supplier. Keep it on the cold room wall. Train your workers on these steps. In an emergency, they should know what to do without calling you. 

Remember, a temperature rise is not a disaster if you act fast. But if you ignore it, you lose money and reputation. So keep your thermometers working, your log book updated, and your phone charged.

lessons.title: Defrosting the Cooling Unit
lessons.body:
Over time, the cooling unit in your cold room builds up frost or ice on the evaporator coils. This happens because moisture in the air freezes on the cold coils. A thick layer of ice (more than 5 mm) acts like a blanket, preventing the unit from cooling efficiently. The compressor runs longer, uses more electricity, and the temperature may rise. So you must defrost regularly. 

How often? In humid African climates, defrost every 2-4 weeks. In drier areas, every 4-6 weeks. Check the coils weekly. If you see white frost or ice, it is time. Many modern units have an automatic defrost cycle, but they can fail. So always check manually. 

Manual defrosting steps: 

1. Turn off the cooling unit at the main switch or thermostat. Do not just turn down the thermostat; turn off power. 

2. Remove all meat from the cold room. Place it in another cold room, or in insulated boxes with ice. Work quickly. 

3. Open the cold room door to let warm air in. You can also place a fan to blow air over the coils. Never use a knife, screwdriver, or hammer to chip ice. You can puncture the refrigerant lines, causing a leak and costly repair. 

4. Place towels or buckets under the unit to catch melting water. 

5. Let the ice melt naturally. This may take 1-2 hours. To speed up, you can use a hairdryer on low heat, but keep it moving and never use hot water directly on the coils. 

6. Once all ice is gone, clean the coils with a soft brush and mild soapy water. Rinse with clean water and dry. 

7. Check the drain pan and drain line. Clear any blockages. 

8. Turn the unit back on. Let it run for 30 minutes to reach the correct temperature (0Â°C to 2Â°C) before putting meat back. 

9. Record the defrost date in your log book. 

If you have an automatic defrost unit, still check monthly. Sometimes the timer or heater fails. If you see ice, do a manual defrost. 

Defrosting is also a good time to check door seals, clean the floor, and inspect for pests. A clean cold room works better and lasts longer. 

In Africa, power cuts can interrupt defrost cycles, leading to more ice. So be extra vigilant. If you cannot defrost because you have no backup storage, do it early in the morning when it is cool, and use ice boxes. Plan ahead. 

Never ignore ice build-up. It costs you money in electricity and can spoil your meat. A 30-minute defrost every few weeks is a small price to pay for reliable cooling.

lessons.title: Keeping a Temperature Log Book
lessons.body:
A temperature log book is a simple notebook where you record the temperature of your cold room at least twice a day. It is a legal requirement in many countries for food safety, and it is your proof that you are handling meat properly. It also helps you spot problems early. 

What to record: Date, time, air temperature, meat temperature (if you probe), and your initials. Also note any events: power cut, defrost, door left open, delivery of new meat, or cleaning. Use a table format. For example: 

Date | Time | Air Temp | Meat Temp | Notes | Initials 

1/5/25 | 7:00 | 1Â°C | 2Â°C | Normal | JM 
1/5/25 | 17:00 | 2Â°C | 3Â°C | Door opened often | JM 

Keep the log book near the cold room, but not inside (it will get damp). Use a pen, not pencil, because pencil fades. If you have a data logger, you can print or download the data and attach it, but still keep a manual log for quick reference. 

Why it matters: If a customer gets sick, health inspectors will ask for your records. If you cannot show them, you may be fined or closed. Also, if you sell meat to hotels or supermarkets, they may require a log book as part of your contract. 

Review your log weekly. Look for patterns: Does the temperature rise every afternoon? Does it drop too low at night? Are there gaps in recording? If you see a problem, fix it. For example, if the temperature rises every time the door opens, train staff to be quicker. If it rises at night, maybe the unit needs servicing. 

Keep log books for at least 6 months. Store them in a dry place. You can use a simple exercise book or a printed template. If you have a smartphone, you can use a free app like

to record digitally. But always have a paper backup in case of power loss. 

Train everyone who uses the cold room to fill the log. Make it part of their daily duties. Check the log yourself every week and sign it. This shows your commitment to quality. 

A well-kept log book is a powerful tool. It protects your business, your customers, and your reputation. It also helps you save money by catching small issues before they become big losses. So start today. Buy a notebook, draw a table, and begin recording. Your future self will thank you.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Temperature Control and Monitoring for a 4â10 Beast Cold Room

In a small African meat business â whether you slaughter 4 goats a day in Kano, chill 6 beef quarters in Nakuru, or hold 10 sheep carcasses for a weekend market in Mbarara â the cold room is your bank vault. Every degree of drift is money: weight loss, discolouration, off-odours, rejected orders, and in the worst case, a total loss of a day's kill. This Practical Reference module gives you the working numbers, the tools, the routines, and the paperwork to keep fresh meat safe and saleable between slaughter and sale.

Business-first principle: temperature control is not a technical chore, it is a margin-protection activity. A well-run 4â10 beast room typically holds meat 3â7 days for chilled sale, or builds stock for further processing (sausage, smoked, dried). Every hour above 7 Â°C shortens that window and cuts your price. Every defrost neglected raises your electricity bill. Every missing log entry weakens your case when a buyer, hotel, or regulator asks questions.

1. Ideal Temperature for Fresh Meat Storage

Fresh red meat should be held as close to 0 Â°C as your equipment allows without freezing, and never above 7 Â°C. The internationally accepted chilled storage band for fresh beef, goat, sheep and game is â1 Â°C to +2 Â°C for optimum shelf life, with a legal/operational ceiling of +7 Â°C in most food safety frameworks. In practice, small African cold rooms run best at 0 Â°C to +4 Â°C: cold enough to slow bacterial growth sharply, warm enough to avoid surface freezing that dulls colour and damages texture.

Why the range matters commercially:

  • 0â2 Â°C: maximum chilled shelf life, best colour retention, premium butchery and hotel trade.
  • 3â4 Â°C: practical working band for busy rooms with frequent door opening; still safe for several days.
  • 5â7 Â°C: short-term only â sell or process within 24â48 hours; higher drip loss and faster spoilage.
  • Above 7 Â°C: rapid bacterial multiplication; meat becomes a food safety risk and a commercial liability.

2. Using a Thermometer and Data Logger

You need two layers of measurement: a handheld probe thermometer for spot checks (air, surface, deep muscle, incoming carcasses) and a data logger (or a min-max thermometer) to record continuously. In many African towns, calibrated digital probe thermometers are available through veterinary supply shops, agro-dealers, or food-safety NGOs; simple USB data loggers are increasingly common and cost-effective.

Probe thermometer â correct use:

  1. Sanitise the probe with an alcohol wipe before and after each use.
  2. For air temperature, hold the probe in the middle of the room, away from the door and the evaporator, for at least 60 seconds.
  3. For meat temperature, insert into the thickest part of the muscle, avoiding bone and fat.
  4. Wait for the reading to stabilise, then record the value and time.
  5. Check calibration monthly in an ice-water bath (0 Â°C Â± 1 Â°C).

Data logger â correct use:

  1. Place the logger in the warmest part of the room (usually near the door or at the top), not next to the evaporator.
  2. Set the interval to 5â15 minutes for a 4â10 beast room.
  3. Download or read the data at least once a day; keep the record.
  4. Set alarm thresholds at +5 Â°C (warning) and +7 Â°C (critical).

3. Checking Temperature Twice Daily

Twice-daily checks are the minimum practical standard for a small cold room. In hot African climates â where ambient temperatures can exceed 35 Â°C and power may fluctuate â twice daily is not optional, it is risk management.

  • Morning check (before opening for business): record air temperature, meat surface temperature of one representative carcass, and power status.
  • Evening check (after last sale / before closing): record air temperature, check door seals, and note any rise during the day.
  • If the room is opened frequently during the day, add a midday spot check.

Each check should take under five minutes and be written into the log book immediately â not reconstructed from memory later.

4. What to Do When Temperature Rises

A temperature rise is a business event. Act in this order:

  1. Confirm the reading. Re-check with a second thermometer; a faulty probe is common.
  2. Check the power. Is there a power cut, tripped breaker, or loose plug? Restore if safe.
  3. Check the door. Was it left open? Close it and monitor for 30 minutes.
  4. Check the evaporator. Is it iced up? If yes, start defrost (see lesson 5).
  5. Check airflow. Are carcasses stacked too tightly against the evaporator or walls? Re-space them.
  6. Check refrigerant. If the compressor runs but the room does not cool, you may have a gas leak â call a technician.
  7. Protect the meat. If temperature exceeds 7 Â°C for more than 2 hours, prioritise sale or processing of the most vulnerable cuts; consider moving meat to a backup chiller or using ice.
  8. Record everything. Time, temperature, action taken, and outcome.

â  SAFETY WARNING

Never sell or process meat that has been held above 7 Â°C for more than 2 hours, or above 10 Â°C for more than 1 hour. Do not attempt to "rescue" suspect meat by re-chilling it â bacterial toxins may already be present and are not destroyed by cold or normal cooking. Discard or, where permitted, send for inspection. Selling temperature-abused meat can cause serious illness, destroy your reputation, and lead to closure by authorities.

5. Defrosting the Cooling Unit

Ice build-up on the evaporator is the most common cause of slow cooling in small cold rooms. A 5 mm ice layer can noticeably reduce efficiency; 10 mm or more can raise room temperature by several degrees and increase electricity consumption.

Defrost procedure:

  1. Move meat to a backup chiller or insulated box with ice.
  2. Switch off the cooling unit (or activate defrost mode if available).
  3. Allow ice to melt naturally; never use a knife, screwdriver, or hammer to chip ice â you can puncture the coil and lose refrigerant.
  4. Collect meltwater and clean the floor; check the drain line is clear.
  5. Clean the evaporator and fan with a soft brush or cloth.
  6. Switch on, let the room reach 0â4 Â°C, then return the meat.
  7. Record the defrost date, duration, and any issues.

Frequency: every 2â4 weeks in humid conditions; every 4â6 weeks in dry conditions; immediately if ice is visible on the coil.

6. Keeping a Temperature Log Book

The log book is your evidence of due diligence. It protects you with buyers, hotels, regulators, and insurers. Keep it simple, keep it consistent, and keep it on site.

Minimum columns: date, time, air temperature, meat temperature, power status, action taken, initials.

Retention: at least 12 months. In many jurisdictions, food businesses are expected to keep temperature records for a similar period; check your local authority.

Data Tables

Table 1. Target temperatures by product and stage (fresh meat, 4â10 beast operation).

Stage / product Target temp (Â°C) Maximum (Â°C) Notes
Post-slaughter carcass chilling0 to +2+7Reach +7 Â°C within 24 h; ideally +2 Â°C within 24â48 h
Chilled beef / goat / sheep storageâ1 to +2+7Optimum shelf life; 0â4 Â°C practical in small rooms
Chilled offal (liver, kidney)0 to +2+4More perishable; sell within 2â3 days
Chilled minced meat0 to +2+4Sell or freeze within 24â48 h
Frozen storage (if applicable)â18 or colderâ15Keep freezer separate from chiller

Sources: FAO/WHO guidance on meat chilling; Codex Alimentarius CAC/RCP 58-2005; UK FSA chilled storage guidance (adapted for small-scale operations).

Table 2. Twice-daily temperature log template (example week).

Date Time Air temp (Â°C) Meat temp (Â°C) Power Action / comments Initials
Mon 0107:30+2+3OKNormalJM
Mon 0118:00+3+4OKDoor seal checkedJM
Tue 0207:30+4+5OKRoom opened early; monitorJM
Tue 0218:00+2+3OKRecoveredJM
Wed 0307:30+8+8Power cut 04:00â06:00Evaporator iced; defrosted; meat moved to backupJM
Wed 0318:00+2+3OKBack to normal; discard affected offalJM
Thu 0407:30+1+2OKNormalJM

Template based on standard HACCP monitoring record practice; adapt to your local authority's requirements.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Target room temperature 0â4 Â°C; never exceed 7 Â°C.
  • â Calibrate probe thermometer monthly in ice water (0 Â°C Â± 1 Â°C).
  • â Check and record temperature twice daily â morning and evening.
  • â Keep data logger in the warmest part of the room, not near the evaporator.
  • â Defrost when ice reaches 5 mm, or every 2â4 weeks.
  • â Never chip ice with a knife â use natural melt only.
  • â Record every temperature rise, action, and outcome in the log book.
  • â Retain log books for at least 12 months.
  • â If meat exceeds 7 Â°C for over 2 hours, do not sell â discard or inspect.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Guidelines for the Humane Slaughter of Animals and Meat Hygiene
  • FAO â Small-scale Meat Processing: A Manual for Developing Countries
  • Codex Alimentarius â Code of Hygienic Practice for Meat (CAC/RCP 58-2005)
  • UK Food Standards Agency â Chilled Storage and Transport of Food
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual

Bottom line for your business: a 4â10 beast cold room lives or dies on discipline. Two checks a day, a calibrated thermometer, a working data logger, a clean evaporator, and an honest log book will protect your meat, your customers, and your margin. In a market where buyers increasingly ask for proof of safe handling, that log book is not paperwork â it is a sales tool.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for fresh meat storage?
quiz.explanation: Fresh meat should be stored between -1Â°C and 2Â°C to slow bacterial growth without freezing.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid putting warm meat directly into the cold room?
options: A) It makes the meat tough
B) It raises the room temperature and risks spoiling other meat
D) It causes the door to freeze
quiz.explanation: Warm meat raises the overall temperature, which can allow bacteria to grow on all meat in the room.

quiz.q: What is the recommended relative humidity for fresh meat storage?
quiz.explanation: 85-90% humidity prevents meat from drying out while discouraging mould growth.

quiz.q: How often should you check the cold room temperature at minimum?
quiz.explanation: Twice daily checks (morning and afternoon) are the minimum to catch problems early.

quiz.q: What should you do first if the cold room temperature rises above 4Â°C?
options: B) Check if the door is closed properly
C) Throw away all the meat
quiz.explanation: A common cause is an open or poorly sealed door, so check that first before other steps.

quiz.q: How thick can ice build-up on the evaporator coils before it affects efficiency?
quiz.explanation: More than 5 mm of ice acts as insulation and reduces cooling efficiency.

quiz.q: What tool should you never use to remove ice from the cooling unit?
options: B) A hairdryer on low heat
quiz.explanation: Using a knife or screwdriver can puncture refrigerant lines, causing a costly leak.

quiz.q: What should you record in a temperature log book?
options: B) Date, time, temperatures, and any events
C) Only the date and your name
D) The weight of the meat
quiz.explanation: A complete log includes date, time, air and meat temperatures, notes on events, and initials.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calibrate your thermometer regularly?
options: A) To make it last longer
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures the thermometer gives correct readings, which is critical for food safety.

quiz.q: What is the boiling point of water in Nairobi (1,795 m above sea level)?
quiz.explanation: Boiling point drops about 1Â°C for every 300 m elevation, so in Nairobi it is about 94Â°C.

quiz.q: How often should you defrost a cold room in a humid African climate?
quiz.explanation: In humid conditions, defrost every 2-4 weeks to prevent ice build-up.

quiz.q: What is a data logger?
options: A) A person who records temperatures
B) A device that records temperature over time
quiz.explanation: A data logger is an electronic device that automatically records temperature at set intervals.

quiz.q: What should you do if the temperature is above 7Â°C for more than 2 hours?
options: C) Cook or discard the meat
D) Add ice to the cold room
quiz.explanation: Meat held above 7Â°C for over 2 hours may be unsafe; it should be cooked immediately or discarded.

quiz.q: Where should you place a thermometer in the cold room?
options: C) In at least two places: near the door and at the back
quiz.explanation: Temperature can vary by 2-3Â°C across the room, so use multiple thermometers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a min-max thermometer?
options: A) To show the current temperature only
B) To show the highest and lowest temperatures since last reset
quiz.explanation: A min-max thermometer records the extreme temperatures, helping you detect fluctuations.

quiz.q: What should you do before putting meat back after defrosting?
options: A) Let the unit run for 30 minutes to reach 0-2Â°C
D) Wipe the coils with oil
quiz.explanation: The unit must cool down to the correct temperature before meat is returned to avoid spoilage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a temperature log book?
options: A) It is required by law and helps spot problems
B) It is a good place to store recipes
C) It helps you remember to buy meat
D) It is used to calculate electricity bills
quiz.explanation: Log books are often legally required and provide early warning of temperature issues.

quiz.q: How long should you keep temperature log books?
quiz.explanation: Keep log books for at least 6 months for health inspections and your own records.

quiz.q: What is the first step in manual defrosting?
options: B) Turn off the cooling unit
quiz.explanation: Turn off the power to the cooling unit before starting defrosting to ensure safety.

quiz.q: What can you use to speed up defrosting?
options: C) A hairdryer on low heat
quiz.explanation: A hairdryer on low heat can safely speed up melting without damaging the coils.

quiz.q: What is the ideal meat temperature when you probe it?
quiz.explanation: Meat temperature should also be within -1Â°C to 2Â°C for safe fresh storage.

quiz.q: Why should you clean the probe after each use?
options: C) To make it last longer
quiz.explanation: Cleaning prevents bacteria from being transferred from one piece of meat to another.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have a power cut and no generator?
options: A) Open the door to let cool air out
B) Use ice blocks or dry ice to keep the room cool
D) Turn off the cold room
quiz.explanation: Ice blocks or dry ice can help maintain low temperatures during a power outage.

quiz.q: How often should you review your temperature log?
quiz.explanation: Weekly reviews help you spot patterns and address issues before they become serious.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your cold room door seals need replacing?
options: A) The door is hard to open
B) You feel cold air escaping around the door
D) The door has a window
quiz.explanation: If cold air escapes, the seals are likely worn and need replacement.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see ice on the evaporator coils?
quiz.explanation: Ice reduces efficiency, so defrost the unit promptly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended frequency for calibrating a thermometer?
quiz.explanation: Monthly calibration ensures the thermometer remains accurate.

quiz.q: What is an ice bath used for?
quiz.explanation: An ice bath provides a known reference temperature of 0Â°C for calibration.

quiz.q: What should you do if the temperature rises but you cannot find the cause?
quiz.explanation: If basic checks do not solve the issue, a qualified technician should inspect the system.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep the cold room door closed?
options: A) To keep the light off
B) To prevent cold air from escaping and warm air from entering
D) To keep the meat from falling out
quiz.explanation: Frequent door openings cause temperature fluctuations and put meat safety at risk.
